definition: Pejorative means expressing contempt or disapproval; describing a term that carries a negative, insulting sense.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word pejorative. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know pejorative should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The style guide warns reporters that 'bureaucrat' can read as pejorative and suggests 'civil servant' in neutral copy.
Unflattering is weaker than pejorative: an unflattering description is merely not kind, while a pejorative one carries built-in contempt.
Abusive is stronger than pejorative — abusive language attacks a person outright, while a pejorative term belittles more quietly, sometimes in a single word.

Derogatory describes any remark, gesture, or tone that shows a low opinion of its target — an aimed put-down in the moment. Pejorative is a property of the word itself: a pejorative term carries its sneer built in, so that merely using it signals contempt. A comment is derogatory; a label is pejorative.

Belittling means making someone or something seem small or unimportant, usually through dismissive mockery that stops short of outright assault. A pejorative term does that same work in a single word — the label itself belittles its subject, whatever sentence it sits in.

Linguists call it pejoration when a word's meaning drifts downhill over time — straight from pejor, 'worse,' the same root that makes a pejorative term one that talks a person down.
Pejorative means expressing contempt or disapproval; describing a term that carries a negative, insulting sense.

The astronomy club's newsletter once referred to amateur stargazers as 'dabblers.' Letters poured in: members who spent freezing nights logging variable stars did not consider themselves casual toy-scientists.
The editor had meant it affectionately, but she recognized the problem — whatever her intent, the word landed as a put-down.
The next issue replaced it with 'independent observers' and carried an apology for the pejorative label.
'Dabblers' lands as a belittling put-down regardless of the editor's intent — a term carrying that built-in disapproval is what pejorative describes.
formal; linguistic and editorial

Keep pejorative apart from its unit-mates: a pejorative is a single disparaging term or label (dictionaries even tag entries 'often pejorative'), while invective is a whole stream of insulting language, and vindictive describes a revenge-hungry person, not words.

When the natural history museum began revising its oldest galleries, the curators started with the labels, not the fossils.
Placards from the 1950s described certain tools as the work of 'primitive' peoples, and that one word stopped the revision committee cold.
The committee's linguist argued that 'primitive' had become pejorative: whatever the writer intends, the label itself now carries a sneer, ranking whole cultures as lesser.
A curator objected that the old placards were meant as neutral chronology, not contempt.
The linguist agreed about the intent — and answered that intent no longer travels with the word.
The new labels say 'early' instead.
Visitors, the committee reasoned, should be free to judge the tools without a term that has already judged the makers.
